Abdur Razzak Dobash ------ Petitioner
 Vs.   
Abdul Karim Dobash and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
13. In the reported case, an application was filed by the plaintiff before the trial Court along with the original copy of the award giving rise to a presumption that the Arbitrator consented to the filing of the award in court by the plaintiff and their Lordships were of the opinion that had the Arbitrator not given his consent, the original copy of the award would not have been handed over to the plaintiff. As the original copy of the award was already filed before the court by the plaintiff it was not necessary for the court to direct the Arbitrator to file the award again and from the above it is found that the provision of section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act was complied with. Mention may be made here that Mr. Khalilur Rahman, learned Counsel representing the opposite parties, also placed reliance on this decision contending that before the impugned order of status quo was passed, the plaintiff filed a signed photo copy of the award in court thus fulfilling the requirement of section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act. Mr. Khalilur Rahman further submits that the order sheet and the feisty of papers filed by the plaintiffs would show that the certified copy of award was filed in court by the plaintiffs before the impugned interim order was passed giving it jurisdiction to act under section 18(1) of the Arbitration Act to prevent the defendant from taking away the money of Yacubally and Sons from the Port Authority and other organizations. Mr. Khalilur Rahman further submits that apart from section 18(1) of the Arbitration Act, the court also has jurisdiction to pass an order of injunction under section 41(a)(4) of the Arbitration Act read with the second schedule thereof and the Civil Procedure Code. Mr. Khalilur Rahman also argues that an order of injunction passed under Order 43 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the instant application under section 115(1) of the CPC is not maintainable. He further submits that the plaintiff himself can file the award in court for making it a Rule of the court under section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act more so because there is no allegation that the Arbitrator has not given the plaintiffs the authority to file the award in court. As regards jurisdiction of the court Mr. Rahman submits that section 31(4) of the Arbitration Act gives exclusive jurisdiction to the Court in view of the earlier Misc Case No. 9 of 1997 which was filed seeking an order of injunction under section 41(b) of the said Act. This jurisdiction has been conferred on this court specifically notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force which is suggestive of the fact that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law regarding the pecuniary jurisdiction, this court and this court alone shall have the jurisdiction to deal with this arbitration. Mr. Khalilur Rahman further submits that there was no irregularity in filing Misc. Case No. 28 of 1997 in the court of the Senior Assistant Judge inspite of the fact that the Arbitration award involved an amount far in excess of the pecuniary jurisdiction of the said court. Mr. Khalilur Rahman argues that his case is covered by section 31(1) of the Arbitration Act which provides that subject to the provisions of this Act an award may be filed in any Court having a jurisdiction in the matter to which the reference relates and cited the decision in the case Guru Nanak Foundation, vs. Rattan Singh and Sons reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 2075 in which case their Lordships held that section 31 of the Act provides the forum in which an award may be filed. Sub-section (1) of section 31 provides that an award may be filed in any court having jurisdiction in the matter to which the reference relates. Incorporating in the definition the expression Court as set out in sub-section (1) of section 31 would mean that the award will have to be filed in that court the suit in respect of the dispute involved in the award would have been required to be filed. This is quite consistent with the provision contained in sub-section (2) of section 14. So far there is no difficulty. The scheme disclosed in sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 31 clearly indicates that to the exclusion of all other courts only one court will have jurisdiction to deal with the proceedings incidental to the reference and the arbitration. Sub-section (3) clearly points in this direction when it provides that all applications regarding the conduct of arbitration proceedings or otherwise arising out of such proceedings shall be made to the court where the award has been or may be filed and to no other court. Then comes sub-section (4). It opens with a non-obstante clause and is comprehensive in character. The non-obstante clause excludes anything anywhere contained in the whole Act or in any other law for the time being in force if it is contrary to or inconsistent with the substantive provision contained in sub-section (4). To that extent it carves out an exception to the general question of jurisdiction of the court in which award may be filed elsewhere provided in the Act in respect of the proceedings referred to in sub-section (4). The provision contained in sub-section (4) will have an overriding effect in relation to the filing of the award if the conditions therein prescribed are satisfied. If those conditions are satisfied the court other than the one envisaged in section 14(2) or section 31(1) will be the court in which award will have to be filed. That is the effect of the non obstante clause in sub-section 4 of section 31. Sub-section (4) thus invests exclusive jurisdiction in the court, to which an application has been made in any reference and which that court is. competent to entertain as the court having jurisdiction over the arbitration proceedings and all subsequent applications arising out of reference and the arbitration proceedings shall have to be made in that court and in no other court. Thus sub-section (4) not only confers exclusive jurisdiction on the court to which an application is made in any reference but simultaneously ousts the jurisdiction of any other court which may as well have jurisdiction in this behalf. To illustrate the point, if an award was required to be filed under section 14 read with section 31(1) in any particular court as being the court in which a suit touching the subject matter of award would have been required to be filed, but if any application in the reference under the Act has been filed in some other court which was competent to entertain that application, then to the exclusion of the first mentioned court the latter alone, in view of the overriding effect of the provision contained in section 31(4), will have jurisdiction to entertain the award and the award will have to be filed in that court alone and no other court will have jurisdiction to entertain the same." 

 17. As regards the second contention raised by Mr. Khalilur Rahman that there is no bar for either of the parties to file the award in court provided it is signed by the arbitrator and in the instant case the copy of the award which the plaintiffs filed was duly signed by the arbitrator and handed over to plaintiffs showing that the plaintiff was authorized by the arbitrator to file the award in court and having done so the Assistant. Judge was competent to pass the ad interim order ie status quo under section 18(1) of the Arbitration Act. In support of his contention he placed reliance on the decision reported in 41 DLR 504 in the case of Bajla Rice Mills vs. Bangladesh which was also relied on by Dr. Rafiqur Rahman. In the reported case the plaintiff filed the original copy of the award duly signed by the arbitrator and their Lordships held that had the arbitrator not given his consent for the award to be filed through the plaintiff, the original copy could not have come to the plaintiff. So the obvious presumption is that the plaintiff was authorised by the arbitrator to file the award in court which, in the instant case, is lacking because there was an application filed by the plaintiff for directing the arbitrator to file the award in court but before that was complied with by the Arbitrator, the plaintiff obtained a signed photo copy attested by the arbitrator himself, and filed the same in court, Dr. Rafiqur Rahman has laid emphasis on the requirement of filing the original copy of the award to imply that the arbitrator had given authority to the plaintiff to file the same in court but in the present case the arbitrator having retained the original copy of the award with himself, the same could not be said to have been filed in court and the filing of the photo copy attested by the arbitrator cannot bring the instant case within the protective umbrella provided in the case reported in 41 DLR and this argument of Dr. Rafiqur Rahman has considerable force. The next contention of Mr. Khalilur Rahman as regards the maintainability of a provisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order passed under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure it is seen that under Order 43 rule 1 of CPC orders passed under rules 1, 2, 4 and 10 of Order 39 of the Code have been made appealable whereas in the instant case the impugned order was passed under Order 39 rule 3 of the CPC and not under the rules mentioned in rule 1 of Order 43 and in that view of the matter, the contention that an appeal lies against an order passed under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be accepted.
